message.content:
Below is a concise summary of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is not legal advice; if you need help with a specific situation, consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit. | Keep a written receipt when you pay the deposit. Ask for a written itemized list of any deductions before you move out. | | **Notice Requirements** | • 30‑day notice to terminate a month‑to‑month lease.
• 60‑day notice if the landlord wants to raise rent or change the lease terms.
• 90‑day notice if the landlord wants to end the tenancy for reasons other than non‑payment of rent. | Get notices in writing and keep copies. If you receive a notice that violates the required time frame, you may refuse to leave until the proper notice period has elapsed. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | Landlords must maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary condition and make necessary repairs within a reasonable time after being notified. | Document problems (photos, emails). If the landlord fails to act, you can withhold rent, repair and deduct, or file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA). | | **Rent Payment** | Rent is due on the date specified in the lease. Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. Keep proof of payment. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | Report disturbances promptly. If the landlord repeatedly interferes, you may seek a court order. | | **Privacy / Entry** | Landlords must give at least 24 hours written notice before entering, except in emergencies. | Keep a log of all entries. If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint. | | **Discrimination** | Under federal Fair Housing laws and Texas statutes, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Eviction Process** | Evictions must follow the Texas Property Code: a written notice (usually 3 days for non‑payment), filing a lawsuit, and obtaining a judgment. | Do not leave the property before the court orders it. If you’re served with a notice, respond promptly—often you can negotiate a settlement. | | **Lease Termination** | You can terminate a lease early by giving proper notice and paying any agreed-upon penalties. | Review your lease for any “early termination” clauses. Some leases allow you to sublet or assign the unit with landlord approval. | | **Legal Assistance & Resources** | • Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) – consumer complaints, mediation services.
• Local tenant‑rights groups (e.g., Texas Tenants Union).
• Legal Aid of North Texas, Lone Star Legal Aid, etc. | Contact these organizations for free or low‑cost legal help. | ### Quick Checklist for Your Next Move 1. **Read your lease carefully** – note the notice periods, security deposit rules, and any special clauses (subletting, pets, late fees). 2. **Document everything** – photos, emails, text messages, receipts. 3. **Keep copies of all correspondence** – especially notices from the landlord. 4. **Know the deadlines** – if you’re moving out, start the notice process early. 5. **Ask for a written itemized statement** of any deductions from your security deposit when you move out. --- #### Want a Sample Lease? If you’re drafting a new lease or want to see how a standard Texas lease looks, let me know the type of lease (e.g., month‑to‑month, fixed‑term) and the parties involved, and I can generate a template for you.
message.reasoning: The user asks: "What are my rights as a tenant in the state of Texas?" They want information about tenant rights. We can provide general info. But we might also offer to generate a contract. The user didn't ask for a contract. So we just answer. No tool needed. Provide overview: security deposit limits, notice requirements, habitability, eviction process, etc. Also mention resources.
